questions.text: An infant on a nasal cannula has an SpO₂ of 86% and an FiO₂ requirement of 70%. An ABG shows PaO₂ 48 mmHg and PCO₂ 45 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Place the patient on NCPAP — this is an oxygenation problem with a normal PCO₂
Intubate immediately because the pH and PCO₂ contraindicate CPAP
Increase the nasal cannula flow and continue to observe
Begin chest compressions and bag-mask ventilation

questions.text: Which set of values represents a CONTRAINDICATION to NCPAP rather than an indication?

answers.text: Respiratory arrest with pH 7.20 and PaCO₂ 55 mmHg — CPAP is not indicated for CO₂ removal
PaO₂ of 45 mmHg on supplemental oxygen
An FiO₂ requirement greater than 60%
Decreased lung volumes on chest radiograph with RDS

questions.text: Why do premature neonates with stiff, surfactant-deficient lungs require shorter inspiratory and expiratory times than pediatric patients?

answers.text: Their low compliance gives a short time constant, so the lungs fill and empty faster
Their high resistance gives a long time constant, so the lungs fill and empty faster
Their high compliance requires more time to equilibrate airway pressure
Their time constant is unrelated to compliance and resistance

questions.text: A pediatric asthma patient has high airway resistance. How does this affect the respiratory time constant and ventilator settings?

answers.text: The time constant is long, so longer inspiratory and expiratory times are needed to fill and empty the lungs
The time constant is short, so shorter I:E ratios are needed
The time constant is unaffected, so neonatal settings apply
Resistance lowers the time constant, requiring faster rates

questions.text: What is the general upper limit for peak inspiratory pressure on a neonate, and when may it be exceeded?

answers.text: PIP should not exceed 30 cmH₂O, but this can be broken for premature birth or chest-wall rigidity from a fentanyl infusion
PIP should not exceed 20 cmH₂O and may never be exceeded
PIP should not exceed 40 cmH₂O and may be exceeded for any premature infant
There is no upper limit for PIP in neonates

questions.text: On a pressure-controlled neonatal ventilator, what is the relationship between delta P and tidal volume?

answers.text: Delta P is the difference between PIP and PEEP; increasing delta P increases tidal volume
Delta P is the sum of PIP and PEEP; increasing it decreases tidal volume
Delta P equals the PEEP, and it has no effect on tidal volume
Delta P is the FiO₂ setting and controls oxygenation only

questions.text: What tidal volume range is appropriate for a neonate with ARDS or lung injury?

answers.text: 4–5 mL/kg
6–8 mL/kg
8–10 mL/kg
10–12 mL/kg

questions.text: Which inspiratory time setting is appropriate for a neonate?

answers.text: 0.2–0.4 seconds
0.6–0.8 seconds
Up to 1 second, as in pediatrics
1.5 seconds to match a slow rate

questions.text: A neonate develops air collecting within the chest but outside the normal air cells of the lungs, making breathing difficult. This describes which category of complication, and what are examples?

answers.text: Air leak syndromes — pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and PIE, more likely in underdeveloped lungs
Subglottic stenosis — a chronic airway complication
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia — a progressive parenchymal disease
Transient tachypnea of the newborn — retained lung fluid

questions.text: Which combination of values best indicates a successful outcome of mechanical ventilation in a neonate?

answers.text: PaO₂ > 50 mmHg with FiO₂ < 60%, reversal of respiratory acidosis to a pH > 7.25, and reduced work of breathing
PaO₂ > 100 mmHg with FiO₂ of 80% and a pH of 7.20
PaCO₂ maintained above 70 mmHg with a pH of 7.15
An SpO₂ of 99% on 100% FiO₂ regardless of work of breathing
